slides.text: A computer is just a machine that takes input, processes it, and produces output.

slides.headline: Analog vs digital

posts.title: Von Neumann vs Harvard: Two Ways to Build a Computer

slides.headline: Von Neumann architecture
slides.text: In the Von Neumann architecture, instructions and data share the same memory and the same pathway — simple, but it creates a bottleneck.

slides.headline: Harvard architecture
slides.text: The Harvard architecture gives instructions and data separate memory and separate pathways, so the CPU can fetch both at once.

slides.headline: Why it matters today
slides.text: Most everyday computers use a Von Neumann design; many microcontrollers and DSPs use Harvard-style designs for speed.

posts.title: Bits, Bytes & Binary: The Language of Machines

slides.text: A bit is the smallest unit of information a computer understands — a single 0 or a single 1.

slides.headline: Bytes
slides.text: Group 8 bits together and you get a byte — enough combinations to represent a single character.

slides.headline: Binary
slides.text: Binary is a number system with only two digits, 0 and 1 — everything a computer does is built from it.

slides.headline: Decimal to Binary
slides.text: Converting decimal to binary means repeatedly dividing by 2 and reading the remainders backward.

slides.headline: Binary to Decimal
slides.text: Converting binary to decimal means multiplying each digit by its power of 2 and adding the results.

slides.text: Hexadecimal packs 4 bits into a single digit, making long binary strings much shorter for humans to read.

posts.title: Logic Gates: How Computers Think

slides.headline: Logic gates
slides.text: Logic gates are tiny electronic switches that make decisions — the building blocks of everything a computer computes.

slides.headline: AND gate
slides.text: An AND gate only outputs 1 if both inputs are 1 — like needing two keys turned together to open a door.

slides.headline: OR gate
slides.text: An OR gate outputs 1 if either input is 1 — like a room with two light switches, either one turns the light on.

slides.headline: NOT gate
slides.text: A NOT gate simply flips the input — 1 becomes 0, and 0 becomes 1.
slides.vibe: two-column split, contrasting halves, one key difference each side

slides.headline: XOR gate
slides.text: An XOR gate outputs 1 only when the inputs are different — a gate that checks for disagreement.

slides.headline: How logic gates create computation
slides.text: Chain enough simple gates together, and you can build addition, memory, and eventually everything a CPU does.
